title: Fast and Sure-ious Quantum Process Tomography
authors: A. Afham, Sayantan Sen, Marco Tomamichel
abstract: Quantum process tomography (QPT) protocols are often designed by lifting quantum state tomography (QST) protocols through the Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism, at the cost of an extra step enforcing the trace-preserving (TP) constraint. Existing approaches fall into two classes. The folklore partial normalization, which sandwiches the density estimate between inverse square roots of its input marginal, has a closed form but is used as a heuristic, its only analyses being asymptotic and losing a factor polynomial in the dimension. Projection-based methods are principled but have no closed forms and scale poorly with dimension. We resolve this dichotomy by showing that the partial normalization is the exact projection onto the Choi states of quantum channels in fidelity (equivalently in Bures or purified distance). Consequently, any QST algorithm with guarantees in fidelity lifts to a QPT algorithm that inherits its sample complexity, through a single closed-form congruence that preserves the Choi rank and is computed in Kraus form without any eigendecomposition of Choi dimension. We lift two single-copy protocols and prove that the non-adaptive one (Fidelity Projected Least Squares) recovers the Choi rank and reaches infidelity $\varepsilon$ from a number of channel uses proportional to $1/\varepsilon$. Numerically, for channels of low Choi rank, it improves on the state-of-the-art projected least squares in accuracy, and by orders of magnitude in the time and memory of the TP-regularization step and of the returned estimate.
summary: This paper develops a theoretically rigorous and computationally efficient method for Quantum Process Tomography (QPT). It proves that a simple, closed-form partial normalization heuristic is mathematically equivalent to the optimal fidelity projection onto the set of physical quantum channels. This breakthrough allows QPT algorithms to inherit the favorable sample complexity guarantees of state tomography while avoiding the computational bottlenecks of traditional semidefinite programming methods.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of Quantum Process Tomography (QPT), which requires estimating an unknown quantum channel while enforcing the trace-preserving (TP) constraint.
main_result: The authors prove that the standard 'folklore partial normalization' heuristic is mathematically equivalent to the exact projection onto the set of valid Choi states using fidelity, allowing QST algorithms to be directly lifted to QPT with inherited sample complexity.
method: The core method involves establishing the mathematical equivalence between the partial normalization and the fidelity projection, enabling the use of closed-form, computationally efficient regularization techniques for QPT.
model_or_system: The system under study is an unknown quantum channel $\Phi: \mathcal{L}(A) 	o \mathcal{L}(B)$, which is characterized by its Choi state $C(\Phi)$. The estimation process involves reconstructing this state from measurement data.
key_observables: Fidelity ($F$), Choi Rank, Sample Complexity ($N$), and computational runtime/memory usage.
important_parameters: The dimension of the systems ($d_A, d_B$), the target infidelity ($\epsilon$), and the required number of channel uses ($N \propto 1/\epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the fidelity projection is the correct regularization method, which is shown to be equivalent to the partial normalization formula.
figures_summary: Figures compare the runtime of various TP regularization methods (Fidelity projection vs. SDP vs. HIP) against Choi dimension, showing the fidelity projection is significantly faster. Other figures compare rank recovery and infidelity vs. shot count.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical equivalence between partial normalization and fidelity projection. It then applies this result to lift QST protocols to QPT, demonstrating improved performance over existing projection-based methods in terms of speed and accuracy.
why_interesting: This work provides a computationally tractable and theoretically sound method for characterizing open quantum systems (channels), which is fundamental for quantum process characterization in quantum computing and quantum optics.

figures.caption: Figure 1: From state to process tomography. Left, QST: inside the affine space of Hermitian trace-one matrices (rectangle) lies the set of density matrices D(A) (disc). A QST protocol returns an estimate in a small neigh- borhood (red outline) of the true state ρ intersected with density matrices (shaded region). Right, QPT on the bipartite space A ⊗B: the matrices whose A-marginal is maximally mixed form an affine subspace through the maximally mixed state IAB/dAB (green line, dotted outside D(A⊗B)), and its intersection with D(A⊗B) (dashed chord) is the set CA,B of Choi states of channels. A lifted QPT protocol must regularize a QST output to CA,B.
